newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Revellers toast Hong Kong's return to China.
newsitem.headline: Revellers toast Hong Kong's return to China.

text.p: A well-lubricated cheer greeted Hong Kong's reversion to China in the territory's Wan Chai party district as Monday turned into Tuesday and revellers temporarily put aside concerns about Hong Kong's future.

It was business as usual in the girlie bars and expatriate drinking dens of Wan Chai, once a notorious red light district but in recent years better known as a haunt for tourists looking for a taste of the seedier side of the territory's night life.

Despite fears that unruly elements among British expatriates and local Hong Kong Chinese might cause disturbances, the overall atmosphere was unexpectedly placid. Wan Chai police said the streets were "peaceful".

In the Beer Castle bar, Hong Kong Chinese and expatriates mingled happily as the countdown to midnight ended, and all cheered in chorus as televisions showed British soldiers handing control of the former colony to their Chinese counterparts.

"I don't know if I'm happy or not," said Hong Kong-born Danny Lee, 33, who works in transportation. "(Hong Kong's new leader) Tung Chee-hwa is good for business, good for Chinese people," he said, but added: "If the people want to play politics, then we have to wait and see."

Angela Chiu, a 24-year-old Hong Konger who works in advertising, said: "I feel nothing, really -- no difference. There will be no difference when I wake up tomorrow. A lot depends on how the Hong Kong people behave. Human rights can only be protected by the people themselves," she said.

William Wong, mainland-born but now working for a Taiwan transport company, said: "Nothing has changed, except for the threat to human rights. But if you are a businessman, nothing will change. In fact it will get even better for businessmen. It will change if you're a democrat though...."
Wan Chai's reputation as a red light area began in the 1940s and it was made famous by Richard Mason's 1950s novel "The World of Suzie Wong", whose heroine was a Wan Chai prostitute.
The area was traditionally favoured by soldiers and sailors visiting the area looking for beer, tattoos and company.
In Delany's Irish bar, staff dressed in black silk pyjamas and khaki Red Army hats served a mainly British and Irish clientele while the house band played Irish traditional music.
A huge screen behind the band showed the handover ceremony and, while images of Chinese Prime Minister Li Peng's arrival were immediately greeted with boos, punters were philosophical.
"Colonialism is dead and it's time to go back," said Andy Richardson, a 29-year-old technical manager from Gloucestershire, who has lived in Hong Kong for four years.
"There is no doubt that civil liberties will be affected, but this place is a cash cow -- that is why it's going back..."

"Everyone's had plenty of time to see what's coming and I can't really think of anyone -- the sadness happened months ago. I'm just glad we can leave with dignity, because it would have been a sad end otherwise," he added.

Adam Fountain, 22, an electronics engineer from Tasmania, Australia, said: "It's not so much a good or a bad thing as something which had to happen. It's just unfortunate that you can't mix China and civil liberties."
